title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 20: Bayan Muna v. Ermita: Validity of the Calibrated Preemptive Response (CPR) Policy
keywords: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
Department of Interior and Local Government
primary_topics: Chapter 20 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Bayan Muna v. Ermita, in which a unanimous 13-0 Court, through Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna, sustained the constitutionality of Batas Pambansa 880 as a content-neutral regulation of the time, place and manner of assemblies while striking down the Calibrated Preemptive Response policy as a darkness that shrouds freedom.

The Court's treatment of BP 880 as regulation and not prohibition: it is no absolute ban, permits may be denied only on a showing of clear and present danger, the law is neither overbroad nor a prior restraint, and the delegation to mayors carries a precise and sufficient standard.

The remedy the Court fashioned from Section 15 of the law: because only Cebu City's Fuente Osmena had been declared a freedom park, no prior permit may be required in any public park or plaza of a locality that fails to comply within thirty days from finality, subject only to advance notice to the authorities.

The chapter's reproduction of the Court's own summary, which expressly invoked Chief Justice Panganiban's philosophy that in cases involving liberty the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak.
sub_topics: The consolidated Petitions assailed Batas Pambansa 880 -- in toto by some petitioners, and only Sections 4, 5, 6, 12, 13(a) and 14(a) by others -- and the so-called policy of Calibrated Preemptive Response.
BP 880, the Public Assembly Act of 1985, laid down guidelines on permits for public assemblies, permissible conduct of law enforcement authorities, and prohibited acts and penalties.

CPR was announced in a Malacanang press release of September 21, 2005 declaring that the rule of calibrated preemptive response was in force 'in lieu of maximum tolerance' and that unlawful mass actions would be dispersed.

Petitioners argued that BP 880 required a permit regardless of any clear and present danger, curtailed the choice of venue although time and place form part of the message, and was not content-neutral because it did not apply to pro-government mass actions; they also invoked the ICCPR and other human rights treaties.

Against CPR petitioners argued that it was preemptive, unsupported by any statute, contrary to the maximum tolerance mandated by BP 880, and productive of a chilling effect on the right peaceably to assemble; respondents answered that CPR was simply the responsible and judicious use of means allowed by existing laws.

At the April 4, 2006 Oral Argument the Court framed the issues as whether the challenged provisions were content-neutral or content-based, overbroad or vague, a prior restraint, an undue delegation to mayors, or violative of international human rights instruments, and whether CPR was void on its face, void for non-publication, or void as applied to the rallies of September 26 and October 4, 5 and 6, 2005.

Standing was upheld without difficulty, since petitioners' rights as citizens to assemble peaceably and to petition for redress of grievances were directly affected by a law requiring a permit for all who would publicly assemble in the nation's streets and parks.

The Court gave primacy to assembly, petition, speech, expression and the press, calling them the very basis of a functional democratic polity without which all other rights would be meaningless and unprotected.

BP 880 was held not an absolute ban but a time, place and manner regulation, already described as content-neutral in Osmena v. Comelec, applying to all kinds of public assemblies using public places, with maximum tolerance operating for the benefit of all rallyists independently of the content of their expression.

A permit may be denied only on the ground of clear and present danger to public order, safety, convenience, morals or health -- a limitation recognized even under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the ICCPR -- so the law is neither overbroad nor a prior restraint, content being irrelevant to the regulation.

The delegation to mayors was sustained because the law supplies the clear and present danger standard, the phrase 'imminent and grave danger of a substantive evil' meaning substantially the same thing.

Freedom parks: Section 15 required every city and municipality to establish at least one within six months, yet the solicitor general could name only Cebu City's Fuente Osmena, so the Court ruled that thirty days after finality no prior permit may be required in any public park or plaza of a non-complying locality, advance notices still being due to ensure coordination and orderly proceedings.

CPR served no valid purpose: if it meant the same as maximum tolerance it was superfluous, and otherwise it was illegal, maximum tolerance being the highest degree of restraint that the military, police and other peace-keeping authorities should observe.

Where a mayor has failed to act on an application, rallyists who can show an application duly filed two days before the rally may assemble accordingly, the grant of the permit being presumed and the burden falling on the authorities to show a denial.

The Court's own summary, reproduced in full, struck down CPR as confusing the people and being used by some police agents to justify abuses, while sustaining BP 880 and going one step further in safeguarding liberty through the freedom-park deadline.

The disposition: unanimous in sustaining BP 880, in nullifying CPR insofar as it purported to differ from or replace maximum tolerance, and in directing the DILG to secure compliance with Section 15 within thirty days from finality.

stances.claim: The Calibrated Preemptive Response policy had no place in the legal firmament and had to be struck down, because if it meant the same as maximum tolerance it served no valid purpose and if it meant anything else it was illegal, merely confusing the people and being used by some police agents to justify abuses.
stances.rhetorical_move: exhaustive dilemma -- either identical to the statutory standard and superfluous, or different and unlawful -- capped by the metaphor of a darkness that shrouds freedom

stances.claim: Batas Pambansa 880 could not be condemned as unconstitutional, since it does not curtail or unduly restrict freedoms but merely regulates the time, place and manner of assemblies in public places, and the delegation to mayors is valid because it is bounded by the constitutionally sound clear and present danger standard.
stances.rhetorical_move: point-by-point refutation of each facial attack -- content-neutrality, overbreadth, prior restraint, undue delegation -- against the standards named in the Oral Argument

stances.claim: Because a permit requirement without an alternative forum would in effect deny the right itself, localities that fail within thirty days to designate freedom parks under Section 15 must thereafter allow assemblies in all their public parks and plazas on mere advance notice.
stances.rhetorical_move: remedial step beyond the pleadings, justified as going one step further in safeguarding liberty and enforced by a deadline on the DILG

stances.claim: In cases involving liberty the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak, so laws and actions restricting fundamental rights come to the courts with a heavy presumption against their validity and are subjected to heightened scrutiny.
stances.rhetorical_move: the Decision quoting the Chief Justice's own policy addresses as the interpretive premise for the whole ruling

notable_anecdotes: At the Oral Argument the solicitor general admitted that, to his knowledge, only Cebu City had ever declared a freedom park -- Fuente Osmena -- twenty years after BP 880 gave every city and municipality six months to do so.

The CPR policy was announced not in a statute or an executive issuance but in a Malacanang press release of September 21, 2005 stating that calibrated preemptive response was now in force 'in lieu of maximum tolerance.'
The Court quoted the Chief Justice's repeated policy-address vow to uphold the liberty of the people and to nurture their prosperity as the stated reason for striking CPR down.

The Court addressed the familiar street scene of a rally dispersed because the mayor never acted on the application, holding that an application filed two days in advance suffices and that the burden shifts to the authorities to prove a denial.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Bayan Muna v. Ermita, the consolidated challenge to Batas Pambansa 880, the Public Assembly Act of 1985, and to the Calibrated Preemptive Response policy that Malacanang announced in a press release of September 21, 2005 as being in force in lieu of maximum tolerance. Petitioners argued that BP 880 required a permit regardless of any clear and present danger, curtailed the choice of venue although time and place form part of the message, was not content-neutral, and violated international human rights instruments, and that CPR was preemptive, unsupported by statute, contrary to the maximum tolerance the law mandates, and chilling. In a unanimous 13-0 Decision written by Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna, the Court upheld petitioners' standing, affirmed the primacy of assembly, petition, speech, expression and the press as the very basis of a functional democratic polity, and held that BP 880 is not an absolute ban but a content-neutral regulation of the time, place and manner of assemblies, already so described in Osmena v. Comelec. A permit may be denied only on a showing of clear and present danger to public order, safety, convenience, morals or health -- a limitation recognized even under the Universal Declaration and the ICCPR -- so the law is neither overbroad nor a prior restraint, and the delegation to mayors is bounded by a precise and sufficient standard. Because the solicitor general could name only Cebu City's Fuente Osmena as a designated freedom park, the Court ruled that thirty days after finality no prior permit may be required in the public parks and plazas of any non-complying locality, since without an alternative forum to deny the permit is to deny the right. CPR, it held, served no valid purpose if it meant maximum tolerance and was illegal if it meant anything else, and it was struck down as a darkness that shrouds freedom that merely confused the people and was used by some police agents to justify abuses; the DILG was directed to secure compliance with Section 15 within thirty days.
